review_target: client/src/pages/Panel.jsx (diff from commit 6517d72, "feat: task 2 — add/delete foundation"), client/src/pages/Panel.validation.test.js (new), client/package.json / client/package-lock.json (new vitest devDependency) — against user-spec.md, tech-spec.md (Decisions 2/3/6/7, Risks table), and tasks/2.md. Focus areas requested: prototype pollution via computed object keys (`{ [name]: fields }`), transitive dependency risk from the new vitest devDependency, and whether newly-exporting `defaultSettings` changes security posture.
summary: This task adds pure client-side logic only (constants, validation functions, six setState handlers, one small presentational button component, one test file) — no new network calls, no new endpoints, no rendering of user-controlled content yet (that's Wave 3). No injection, XSS, auth, or authorization issues were found in the actual code. The one substantive, actionable finding is dependency-related: package.json pins `vitest: ^2.1.9`, which resolves to 2.1.9 — a version affected by a critical advisory (GHSA-5xrq-8626-4rwp, CVSS 9.8, arbitrary file read/execute when the Vitest UI server is listening), fixed only in 3.2.6+. Practical risk to this project is reduced (devDependency only, never ships to the client bundle; the project's `test`/`npx vitest run` script uses run mode, not `--ui`), but the vulnerable version is real and worth bumping. Separately, I ran the specific prototype-pollution scenario the task asked me to check (`{ [name]: fields }` with `name === "__proto__"`) empirically in Node and confirmed it is NOT exploitable: computed object-literal keys (including inside object spread) always go through normal own-property creation (CreateDataPropertyOrThrow / CopyDataProperties), not the special [[Prototype]]-setting behavior that only applies to a literal, non-computed `__proto__: value` token — so this pattern can at most create a same-named own property that shadows the inherited accessor on that one object instance, never pollute `Object.prototype` or any shared object. I also diffed the pre-task lockfile against the post-task one to separate pre-existing dev-toolchain vulnerabilities (esbuild/vite dev-server CORS, rollup path traversal, @babel/core, previously-vulnerable nanoid/postcss versions) from anything newly introduced by adding vitest — only the vitest CVE itself is new; everything else was already present (and postcss/nanoid actually got quietly upgraded to patched versions as a side effect of vitest's own dependency resolution). Exporting `defaultSettings` (previously module-private) has no runtime security effect: this is client-bundled code, already fully visible in the shipped JS/devtools regardless of the `export` keyword — it only changes what other ES modules (here, the new test file) can import, not what's disclosed.

findings.description: `npm audit` (run inside client/ with the actual committed lockfile) reports vitest@2.1.9 as vulnerable to GHSA-5xrq-8626-4rwp, "When Vitest UI server is listening, arbitrary file can be read and executed" — CVSS 9.8 (critical), affected range `<3.2.6`. The advisory requires the Vitest UI web server to be actively running (`vitest --ui` or equivalent), which this project's `test` script (`"test": "vitest run"`, package.json:10) does not invoke, and no `.vitest`/UI config was added by this task. So the realistic exposure today is low: it's a devDependency (never bundled into the production client build), and the vulnerable code path isn't part of this project's own tooling usage. Confirmed via a before/after `npm audit` diff (checked out the pre-task lockfile at commit 6517d72^ and compared) that this is the only *new* vulnerability introduced by adding vitest — the esbuild/vite dev-server CORS issue (moderate), rollup path-traversal (high), and @babel/core (low) advisories that also show in `npm audit` on the current tree all pre-date this task (already present via the existing `vite`/`tailwindcss` toolchain before Task 2's commit); nanoid and postcss actually moved from vulnerable to patched versions as a byproduct of vitest's own transitive resolution.
findings.recommendation: Bump `vitest` to `^3.2.6` or later (or the current 4.x line) in `client/package.json` before this feature ships, even though it's currently unreachable via this project's own scripts — the caret range `^2.1.9` cannot self-resolve past 2.x, so this requires an explicit version-string change, not just `npm install`/`npm audit fix`. Low urgency (dev-only, unused feature) but easy and worth doing opportunistically; verify `npx vitest run` still passes after the bump since 2.x → 3.x/4.x is a semver-major jump for the test runner.

findings.owasp: A08:2021 - Software and Data Integrity Failures (investigated, not applicable)
findings.description: Investigated the specific scenario requested: can an admin-supplied `name` (e.g. `name === "__proto__"`) achieve prototype pollution via these computed-key object spreads before the settings object is JSON-POSTed to the backend? Verified empirically in Node (matching this project's JS semantics) that it cannot: `{ ...current.garments, [name]: fields }` with `name = "__proto__"` produces an object with an *own* data property literally named `"__proto__"` (confirmed via `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(merged, "__proto__")` → `true`, and `Object.getPrototypeOf(merged) === Object.prototype` → still `true`, i.e. the real prototype chain is untouched). This is because the ECMAScript special-case that lets `{ __proto__: value }` set an object's `[[Prototype]]` only fires for a *literal*, non-computed `__proto__` token in an object initializer — computed keys (`[name]`) and spread properties both go through ordinary `CreateDataPropertyOrThrow`/`CopyDataProperties`, which never invoke that special-case. `JSON.stringify` of the result also confirmed: it serializes as an ordinary `{"__proto__": {...}}` key, which on the Go backend is just a normal `map[string]GarmentConfig` entry (Go has no prototype-chain concept at all, so even if this reached the server as JSON, `json.Unmarshal` treats it as an unremarkable map key). `isDuplicateName`/`Object.keys`/`Object.entries` used elsewhere in this diff also only ever see own enumerable properties, so a `"__proto__"`-named garment behaves consistently (as a normal, if oddly-named, entry) throughout — no bypass of the dedup check, no cross-object or cross-user pollution.
findings.recommendation: None required — no vulnerability. If desired for defense-in-depth/robustness (not a security fix), `isBlankName`/`isDuplicateName` could additionally reject reserved JS identifiers like `__proto__`, `constructor`, `prototype` as garment/operation names to avoid confusing (but not exploitable) downstream behavior if some future code does `garments[selectedName]` lookups — this is a robustness nicety, not a security gap, and out of this task's scope.

findings.description: Confirmed this newly-added `export` keyword has no security implication. `defaultSettings` is a plain client-side fallback/pre-load object with no secrets, tokens, or server-only data — it's the same static pricing template data that was already fully present and readable in the compiled/bundled client JS shipped to every visitor's browser before this change (ES module `export`/`import` only affects which other modules in the source tree can statically reference a binding; it does not change what ends up in, or is discoverable from, the built bundle). The only new consumer is the co-located test file (`Panel.validation.test.js`), which needs the export to assert `defaultSettings.garments`/`defaultSettings.operations` stay in sync with the server's `DefaultUserSettings()`.

This task's diff does not render any user-controlled string into the DOM yet — `DeleteRowButton` renders a fixed "Удалить" label and takes only a boolean + callback, and none of the new validation/handler code touches JSX. No `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, no `innerHTML`, no template-string HTML construction, no `eval`/`new Function` anywhere in the diff. React's default JSX text-child escaping means that when Wave 3 does start rendering admin-entered garment/operation names as row labels, a name like `` would render as inert text, not execute — as long as Wave 3 keeps using ordinary `{name}` JSX interpolation and doesn't introduce `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. Also confirmed the tech-spec's own Risks table already documents, as an accepted pre-existing condition, that garment/operation names flow unescaped into an AI market-feedback prompt server-side (`server/internal/deepseek.go:404-406`) — that backend code path is untouched by this task and remains a self-scoped, already-reviewed acceptance, not something this task changes.
findings.recommendation: None for this task. Forward note for Wave 3's code-reviewer/security-auditor: verify the actual row-rendering JSX for garment/operation names uses plain `{name}` interpolation (not `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` or a raw HTML string), which is the only way this class of risk could be reintroduced.
